Getting started with coda.plot

Marc Comas-Cufí

Source: vignettes/coda-plot.Rmd
coda-plot.Rmd

coda.plot provides simple plots for exploring compositional data. In this type of data, each row describes how a total is distributed among several parts. For example, a mixture may consist of protein, fat, and carbohydrates.

The most important requirement is that all parts must be strictly positive. Rows do not need to sum to 1 or 100: the functions work with relative proportions.

library(coda.plot)
#> Loading required package: coda.base
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'coda.base'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     dist

set.seed(2026)
X <- matrix(rexp(90, rate = 1), ncol = 3)
colnames(X) <- c("Protein", "Fat", "Carbohydrates")
group <- factor(rep(c("Control", "Treatment"), each = 15))

head(X)
#>        Protein       Fat Carbohydrates
#> [1,] 0.3973469 0.7499553     0.3302451
#> [2,] 0.1130610 2.8804064     1.1843942
#> [3,] 1.5074140 0.2041778     2.1363013
#> [4,] 0.8360404 1.8247179     1.7945151
#> [5,] 0.1107380 0.3626434     1.8339835
#> [6,] 4.0741295 0.4318313     0.3468551

A quick ternary diagram

When there are exactly three parts, ternary_plot() is the most direct way to display them. Each point corresponds to a row of X. A point closer to a vertex has a larger relative proportion of the part shown at that vertex.

ternary_plot(X, group = group)

With center = TRUE, the plot is centred on the mean composition. scale = TRUE standardises variability, while show_pc = TRUE adds the first two principal directions of variation.

ternary_plot(X, group = group, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE, show_pc = TRUE)

Building a ternary diagram layer by layer

The modular interface is useful when you want to control each plot element. First, ternary_frame() defines the transformation and labels. Next, ternary_base() creates the triangle, and the add_ternary_*() functions add layers to it.

frame <- ternary_frame(X, labels = c("P", "F", "C"))

p <- ternary_base(frame, show_grid = FALSE)
p <- add_ternary_grid(p, ticks = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75), colour = "grey80")
#> Warning: Duplicated aesthetics after name standardisation: colour
#> Duplicated aesthetics after name standardisation: colour
#> Duplicated aesthetics after name standardisation: colour
p <- add_ternary_points(p, X, group = group, size = 2)
p

add_ternary_path() joins ordered compositions. In this example, the path shows a gradual transition from a protein-rich composition to a carbohydrate-rich composition.

path <- rbind(
  c(8, 1, 1),
  c(6, 2, 2),
  c(4, 3, 3),
  c(2, 3, 5),
  c(1, 2, 7)
)

p <- ternary_base(ternary_frame(path, labels = colnames(X)))
p <- add_ternary_path(p, path, colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1)
add_ternary_points(p, path, colour = "#0072B2", size = 2)

add_ternary_pc() adds principal directions manually. It is the modular equivalent of show_pc = TRUE.

p <- ternary_base(ternary_frame(X, center = TRUE))
p <- add_ternary_points(p, X, group = group)
add_ternary_pc(p, X, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7)

Finally, ternary_coords() returns the coordinates used for plotting. This is useful for preparing annotations or custom ggplot2 layers.

coords <- ternary_coords(frame, X, group = group)
head(coords)
#>          c1        c2        c3         .A         .B         .C        .x
#> 1 0.3973469 0.7499553 0.3302451 0.26892332 0.50756770 0.22350898 0.3579706
#> 2 0.1130610 2.8804064 1.1843942 0.02706193 0.68944514 0.28349292 0.2970239
#> 3 1.5074140 0.2041778 2.1363013 0.39175049 0.05306223 0.55518728 0.7510625
#> 4 0.8360404 1.8247179 1.7945151 0.18765187 0.40956362 0.40278451 0.4966104
#> 5 0.1107380 0.3626434 1.8339835 0.04799329 0.15716776 0.79483896 0.8188356
#> 6 4.0741295 0.4318313 0.3468551 0.83953927 0.08898571 0.07147502 0.4912447
#>           .y   group
#> 1 0.23289442 Control
#> 2 0.02343632 Control
#> 3 0.33926588 Control
#> 4 0.16251129 Control
#> 5 0.04156340 Control
#> 6 0.72706234 Control

Comparing groups with geometric means

geometric_mean_barplot() compares parts across groups. Bars represent deviations from the overall mean; include_boxplot = TRUE also shows the variability among observations.

geometric_mean_barplot(X, group, include_boxplot = TRUE)

With clr_scale = TRUE, calculations use clr coordinates, which are appropriate for interpreting relative differences among parts.

geometric_mean_barplot(X, group, clr_scale = TRUE)

CLR biplot

For compositions with three or more parts, clr_biplot() summarises observations and parts in two dimensions. Nearby points represent similar observations; label directions indicate which parts explain the variation.

X6 <- matrix(rexp(180), ncol = 6)
colnames(X6) <- paste0("Part_", 1:6)
clr_biplot(X6, group = group)
#> Ignoring unknown labels:
#> • shape : ""

The "covariance" type emphasises the covariance structure among parts, so the lengths and angles of the variable rays are the main elements to interpret. The "form" type emphasises the geometry of the observations, so distances between points are the main elements to interpret.

clr_biplot(X6, group = group, biplot_type = "form")
#> Ignoring unknown labels:
#> • shape : ""

If you need to reuse the coordinates, return_data = TRUE returns the observation data, variable data, and plot.

result <- clr_biplot(X6, group = group, return_data = TRUE)
names(result)
#> [1] "obs"  "vars" "plot"

Log-contrast biplot

logcontrast_biplot() displays observations according to two user-defined contrasts. Each column of lc must sum to zero. Here, the first axis compares parts 1 and 2, while the second compares parts 3 and 4.

lc <- cbind(
  `Part 1 / Part 2` = c(1, -1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  `Part 3 / Part 4` = c(0, 0, 1, -1, 0, 0)
)

logcontrast_biplot(X6, lc, group = group)
#> Ignoring unknown labels:
#> • shape : ""

Balance dendrogram

balance_dendrogram() helps interpret a balance basis. The B matrix describes which parts are compared at each split. One can be generated automatically with coda.base::pb_basis().

B <- coda.base::pb_basis(X6, method = "exact")
balance_dendrogram(X6, B, group = group)

Function summary

Function Main use
ternary_plot() Quickly create a complete ternary diagram.
ternary_frame() Define the ternary transformation and labels.
ternary_base() Create the base triangle.
add_ternary_grid() Add grid lines.
add_ternary_points() Add observations.
add_ternary_path() Add a path of ordered compositions.
add_ternary_pc() Add principal component directions.
ternary_coords() Obtain coordinates for custom layers.
geometric_mean_barplot() Compare parts and groups with geometric means.
clr_biplot() Explore observations and parts in clr coordinates.
logcontrast_biplot() Display two user-defined log-contrasts.
balance_dendrogram() Interpret a balance basis.

To get started, ternary_plot() is usually enough for three-part compositions, while clr_biplot() is a good choice for higher-dimensional compositions. The remaining functions offer more control or answer more specific questions.
